slides.title: Learning Outcome
slides.text:
Learning Outcome

•  Understand the concept of trajectory planning in robotic manipulators.
•  Distinguish between joint space and Cartesian space trajectory schemes.
•  Formulate the trajectory planning problem with boundary conditions.
•  Analyze the limitations of linear trajectories and the need for smoothing.
•  Develop and analyze cubic polynomial trajectories.
•  Compute position, velocity, and acceleration profiles
   for joint motion.
•  Develop and analyze higher order polynomial trajectories.
•  Implement trajectory generation using Python for
   visualization and validation.

slides.title: Trajectory Planning
slides.text:
Trajectory Planning :

•  Trajectory planning is a fundamental problem in robot motion control.
•  Given initial and final configurations of a manipulator, the goal is to generate a
   time-parameterized function describing the evolution of joint variables such
   that motion is physically feasible, smooth, and satisfies task constraints.
•  A trajectory is defined as a mapping:
                   𝜃𝑖𝑡, 𝑖= 1,2, … , 𝑛, 𝑡∈0 𝑡𝑓
    where 𝜃𝑖𝑡represents the joint variable of the 𝑖𝑡ℎjoint.
•  The trajectory must satisfy:
    –  Kinematic constraints (joint limits)
    – Dynamic feasibility (bounded torque)
    – Smoothness (continuity in derivatives)


                                                                                                           4

visualInspection.notes: Read joint-time mapping theta_i(t), i=1..n,t in[0,tf]; initial/final configurations, feasibility, constraints, kinematic joint limits, bounded torque and derivative continuity.

slides.title: Path VS Trajectory
slides.text:
Path VS Trajectory                                             T= 𝑡4   T= 𝑡𝑓
•  A path is a geometric description of the robot's motion;          T= 𝑡3
     it specifies the sequence of configurations θ(s)               T= 𝑡2
                                                                    Trajectory   parameterized by a path variable s ∈ [0,1],
   without any information about timing                    T= 𝑡1
                𝜃= 𝜃𝑠, 𝑠∈[0,1]
                                                          T=0           Path
•  A trajectory is a path plus a time parametrization: θ(t) where
    t ∈ [0, 𝑡𝑓]. The trajectory specifies not only where the robot goes, but also
  when it reaches each point. In practice, trajectory planning means
   designing 𝜃(𝑡), ሶ𝜃𝑡and ሷ𝜃𝑡for each joint.
                𝜃= 𝜃𝑡, 𝑡∈0 𝑡𝑓
              𝜃𝑡= 𝜃𝑠𝑡
  The function 𝑠𝑡is called the time-scaling function.

slides.title: Continuity requirements
slides.text:
CONTINUITY REQUIREMENTS — Three levels of smoothness are important:

•  C⁰ Continuity

        lim        lim 𝜃𝑡, 𝜃𝑡is continuous, No jumps in position.                       +      𝑡→𝑡0−𝜃𝑡= 𝑡→𝑡0
•   C¹ Continuity
     lim ሶ𝜃𝑡= lim ሶ𝜃𝑡, ሶ𝜃𝑡is continuous, No velocity discontinuities.
       𝑡→𝑡0−         𝑡→𝑡0+
•  C² Continuity
                  lim        lim ሷ𝜃𝑡, ሷ𝜃𝑡is continuous,                                 +               𝑡→𝑡0−ሷ𝜃𝑡= 𝑡→𝑡0
                  No acceleration discontinuities.
•  From dynamics:  𝜏∝ሷ𝜃, i.e., discontinuous acceleration
     → infinite torque spikes


                                                                                                           6

visualInspection.notes: C0/C1/C2 explicitly match position/velocity/acceleration left/right limits; nested smoothness presumed. Bottom asserts discontinuous acceleration gives infinite torque spikes, which conflicts with finite inertia dynamics and p479 finite discontinuity statement; preserve discrepancy.

slides.title: Continuity Requirements (Contd..)
slides.text:
Continuity Requirements (Contd..)

• From robot dynamics:
          𝜏= 𝑀Θ ሷΘ + 𝑉Θ, ሶΘ + 𝐺Θ
•   If ሷΘ is discontinuous:
   – Torque becomes discontinuous and leads to shocks and vibrations
•   If ሶΘ is discontinuous:
   –  Infinite acceleration required
•  Thus:
   – Minimum: C¹
   – Preferred: C²



                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: Dynamics τ=M(Θ)Θddot+V(Θ,Θdot)+G(Θ); acceleration jump gives torque discontinuity; velocity jump requires ideal infinite/impulsive acceleration. Minimum C1, preferred C2. Must qualify finite model terms and distinguish jump from impulse.

slides.title: Joint Space Schemes
slides.text:
Joint Space Schemes

•   Joint space Schemes refers to the specification of motion directly in terms of
   the generalized coordinates of the manipulator, i.e.,
   the joint variables. The trajectory is expressed as a
   time-varying vector of joint positions:
                                         𝜃1 𝑡
                                        𝜃2 𝑡                𝜃𝑡=
                                                                ⋮
                               𝜃𝑛𝑡
•  Each joint trajectory is independently generated using
   interpolation functions (such as cubic or quintic) satisfying
   boundary conditions on position and velocity:
                  𝜃0 = 𝜃0, 𝜃𝑡𝑓= 𝜃𝑓
                           ሶ𝜃0 = ሶ𝜃0, ሶ𝜃𝑡𝑓= ሶ𝜃𝑓

                                                                                                           9

visualInspection.notes: Joint trajectory vector theta1..thetan; independently interpolated cubic/quintic; specified position/velocity endpoints. Diagram has same endpoints t0/theta0 and tf/thetaf, blue overshoots then undershoots, red initially dips, green monotonic; positions alone do not select one shape.

slides.title: Joint Space Scheme (Continued)
slides.text:
Joint Space Scheme ( Continued .. )

•  The resulting end-effector motion (𝑥) is obtained through forward
   kinematics from joint angles (𝜃):
            𝑥𝑡= 𝑓𝜃𝑡
•  This generally produces a nonlinear and unpredictable path in
   Cartesian space. Since no inverse kinematics is required during
   trajectory generation, the computational complexity is low.
•  Furthermore, continuity in Θ 𝑡, ሶΘ 𝑡  ,and ሷΘ 𝑡
   directly ensures smooth actuator torques
  through the dynamic model:
     𝜏= 𝑀Θ ሷΘ + 𝑉Θ, ሶΘ + 𝐺Θ

                                                                                                          10

visualInspection.notes: Forward kinematics x(t)=f(theta(t)); printed “nonlinear and unpredictable” must mean not directly prescribed, since known f/theta determine motion. Smooth torque claim presumes continuous dynamics and no unmodeled jumps, not arbitrary actuator feasibility.

slides.title: Trajectory Problem Formulation
slides.text:
Joint Space Scheme -Trajectory Problem Formulation :

•  Given:
    Initial joint angle 𝜃0 at 𝑡= 0, and final joint angle 𝜃𝑓 at 𝑡= 𝑡𝑓.
   Optionally, initial and final velocities ሶ𝜃0, ሶ𝜃𝑓may be specified (commonly zero for
    rest-to-rest motion).
•  Find: A smooth trajectory 𝜃𝑡over the interval[0, 𝑡𝑓] such that:
•   It satisfies all boundary conditions
•   It is sufficiently differentiable (at least 𝐶1, preferably 𝐶2)
•  Standard Boundary Conditions (Rest-to-Rest Motion)
  ➢𝜃0 = 𝜃0, 𝜃𝑡𝑓= 𝜃𝑓
  ➢ ሶ𝜃0 = 0, ሶ𝜃𝑡𝑓= 0



                                                                                                          11

visualInspection.notes: Initial/final joint angles and time, optional endpoint velocities, interval[0,tf], minimum C1/preferred C2, rest-to-rest sets both endpoint velocities zero.

slides.title: General Boundary Conditions and Polynomial Count
slides.text:
Joint Space Scheme -Trajectory Problem Formulation (Contd…)
•  General Boundary Conditions (Via-Point Motion)
  ➢ ሶ𝜃0 = 𝜔0, ሶ𝜃𝑡𝑓= 𝜔𝑓
   ➢𝜔0, 𝜔𝑓 :specified initial and final velocities
•    If we choose a polynomial:
          𝜃𝑡= 𝑎0 + 𝑎1𝑡+ 𝑎2𝑡2 + ⋯+ 𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑛
•  Number of coefficients = 𝑛+ 1
•  Number of constraints must equal number of coefficients.
•  Thus:
  ➢2 conditions → linear,
  ➢4 conditions → cubic & 6 conditions → quintic



                                                                                                          12

visualInspection.notes: General endpoint velocities omega0/omegaf need not zero. Polynomial degree n has n+1 coefficients; 2/4/6 counts map linear/cubic/quintic. Printed count-equality statement requires independent compatible constraints for uniqueness, not merely equal raw number.

slides.title: Why Cubic?
slides.text:
Cubic Polynomial :
WHY CUBIC?
• We need to satisfy exactly 4 boundary conditions : 𝜃0  , 𝜃𝑡𝑓, ሶ𝜃0  , ሶ𝜃𝑡𝑓
•  A polynomial of degree n has (n+1) coefficients.
   – Degree 1 (linear): 2 coefficients → only 2 BCs satisfiable.
   – Degree 2 (quadratic): 3 BCs.
   – Degree 3 (cubic): 4 BCs → exactly matches our 4 requirements.
•  GENERAL CUBIC FORM:
    𝜃𝑡= 𝑎0 + 𝑎1𝑡+ 𝑎2𝑡2 + 𝑎3𝑡3





                                                                                                          13

visualInspection.notes: Four endpoint position/velocity conditions require four independent coefficients generically; degrees1,2,3 give2,3,4. General cubic printed. Lower degree can satisfy special compatible data; uniqueness presumes tf>0.

slides.title: Cubic Polynomial Via Point
slides.text:
Cubic Polynomial Via Point :
• We consider joint-space trajectory generation where a sequence
   of via points  𝜃𝑖  at times  𝑡𝑖  is specified.
•  Each segment between consecutive via points is represented by a
   cubic polynomial.
•  The key difficulty is that, while positions are specified at via
   points, velocities are generally not uniquely defined and must be
                            +   assigned or computed. 𝜃𝑡= 𝑎0 + 𝑎1𝑡+ 𝑎2𝑡2                                              𝑎3𝑡3





                                                                                                          14

visualInspection.notes: Via points theta_i at t_i, one cubic between consecutive points; via velocities not fixed by positions alone and must assigned/computed. Segment-local versus global time must be explicitly distinguished in using zero-time formulas.

slides.title: Methods of Joint Velocity Profile Generation
slides.text:
Methods of Joint Velocity Profile Generation :

•  For a single segment between 𝑡𝑖 and 𝑡𝑖+1 ,we use:
           𝜃𝑡= 𝑎0 + 𝑎1𝑡+ 𝑎2𝑡2 + 𝑎3𝑡3
•  To uniquely determine the four coefficients, we require four boundary
   conditions. For multi-segment trajectories, continuity constraints must be
   enforced at via points.
•  The central issue becomes: how to determine velocities at via points so that
   the trajectory is smooth and physically realizable.
•  There Three approaches:
    ❑User-specified velocities (Cartesian → joint mapping)
    ❑Heuristic velocity assignment
    ❑Acceleration-continuous spline formulation


                                                                                                          20

visualInspection.notes: Three methods explicitly listed: user-specified Cartesian-to-joint velocities, heuristic assignment, acceleration-continuous spline. Four BCs for each cubic; multisegment joins need enforced continuity. Segment duration/local time must not be mistaken for global endpoint time.

slides.title: Higher-Order Polynomial Trajectories (Quintic)
slides.text:
Higher-Order Polynomial Trajectories (Quintic)

•  The general form is:
  ➢𝜃𝑡= 𝑎0 + 𝑎1𝑡+ 𝑎2𝑡2 + 𝑎3𝑡3 + 𝑎4𝑡4 + 𝑎5𝑡5
•  Boundary conditions:
  ➢𝜃0 = 𝜃0, ሶ𝜃0 = ሶ𝜃0, ሷ𝜃0 = ሷ𝜃0
  ➢𝜃𝑡𝑓= 𝜃𝑓, ሶ𝜃𝑡𝑓= ሶ𝜃𝑓, ሷ𝜃𝑡𝑓= ሷ𝜃𝑓
•  Velocity and acceleration:
  ➢ ሶ𝜃𝑡= 𝑎1 + 2𝑎2𝑡+ 3𝑎3𝑡2 + 4𝑎4𝑡3 + 5𝑎5𝑡4
  ➢ ሷ𝜃𝑡= 2𝑎2 + 6𝑎3𝑡+ 12𝑎4𝑡2 + 20𝑎5𝑡3
•  This yields a system of 6 linear equations in 6 unknowns,
   which can be solved uniquely.


                                                                                                          21

visualInspection.notes: Six coefficients a0..a5, endpoints position/velocity/acceleration, correct first and second derivatives (4,5 and12,20 coefficients); six linear equations unique for distinct endpoints tf>0, not from equation count alone.

   at a constant rate from 𝜃0to 𝜃𝑓over a duration 𝑡𝑓.

   a first-order polynomial:
              𝜃𝑡= 𝑎0 + 𝑎1𝑡

•   Final Linear Trajectory Equations

slides.title: Critical Drawbacks
slides.text:
Critical Drawbacks

•  Velocity Discontinuity at Endpoints :

                                          𝜃𝑓−𝜃0
   – At 𝑡= 0−: ሶ𝜃= 0 and At 𝑡= 0+: ሶ𝜃=   ≠0
                                                      𝑡𝑓
   –  Sudden jump in velocity, Δሶ𝜃≠0 →not 𝐶1continuous
•   Infinite Torque Requirement :
   – From dynamics: 𝜏∝ሷ𝜃 At 𝑡= 0 and 𝑡= 𝑡𝑓: ሷ𝜃→∞
   – Equivalent to impulse , Physically impossible for real actuators
•   Conclusion :
   – Linear trajectory satisfies only: 𝐶0 continuity,
   – Does not satisfy 𝐶1
   – Not suitable for smooth robotic motion without modification(e.g., blending)

slides.title: Numerical Example
slides.text:
Numerical Example :

•  Problem Statement
   o A single revolute joint of a robot manipulator is required to move smoothly
      from an initial angular position of 𝜃0 = 10∘at time 𝑡= 0 to a final angular
       position of 𝜃𝑓= 70∘at time 𝑡= 𝑡𝑓= 5 s. The motion must start and end at
        rest, meaning that the initial and final joint velocities are zero, i.e., ሶ𝜃0
    = 0 and ሶ𝜃𝑡𝑓= 0.
•  Solution
  ▪We assume a cubic polynomial trajectory of the form:
    ➢𝜃𝑡= 𝑎0 + 𝑎1𝑡+ 𝑎2𝑡2 + 𝑎3𝑡3

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary
•  A trajectory defines joint motion 𝜃𝑡 over time while satisfying boundary
   conditions and smoothness requirements
•   Joint space planning is simple and efficient, while Cartesian space planning
   provides precise path control but requires inverse kinematics
•  Linear trajectories are not practical due to velocity discontinuity and infinite
   acceleration
•  Cubic polynomial trajectories ensure smooth position and
   velocity with continuous acceleration
•  Higher-order polynomials (e.g., Quintic) allow
   specification of acceleration at endpoints, achieving
   𝐶2continuity across segments



                                                                                                          30

visualInspection.notes: Repeats planning comparison/linear drawbacks; cubic continuous-acceleration wording needs within-segment versus joins qualification. Quintic supports prescribed endpoint acceleration and C2 joins only when adjacent position/velocity/acceleration values match.

sourceIssues.handling: Use the equation θ(t)=θ(s(t)) to define time scaling, which preserves a given path. The schematic does not justify claiming time scaling changes geometry.

sourceIssues.handling: Question-level conflict resolution supplies a finite-inertia counterexample and distinguishes velocity-step acceleration impulses. Compare the more accurate finite-discontinuity wording on p479.

sourceIssues.finding: The table abbreviates Cartesian IK by f⁻¹ and says joint-space planning requires no IK.
sourceIssues.handling: State joint boundary data are already available; f⁻¹ denotes a feasible selected IK branch, not a unique global inverse.

sourceIssues.finding: Known joint trajectories are called unpredictable in task space, and smooth torque is guaranteed without model qualifications.
sourceIssues.handling: Distinguish unprescribed geometry from unknown geometry; explicitly require continuous dynamic terms and absence of external/friction jumps for a torque-continuity guarantee.

sourceIssues.finding: Constraint count is stated as an equality without rank, compatibility or special-case qualifications.
sourceIssues.handling: Use independent boundary conditions and T>0 for unique cubic/quintic solutions. Test a compatible linear special case separately.

sourceIssues.finding: The printed maximum-velocity formula omits the sign qualification for negative displacement.
sourceIssues.handling: Use the printed expression for D>0; for D<0 identify the signed minimum and use absolute displacement for peak speed. Treat D=0 separately.

sourceIssues.finding: The C0-only statement concerns linear motion with stationary segments before and after, not a polynomial on its own interval.
sourceIssues.handling: All endpoint-jump questions explicitly include stationary holds and nonzero displacement; distinguish bounded finite transitions from ideal impulses.

sourceIssues.finding: The summary describes cubic continuous acceleration and quintic C2 across segments without explicit matching qualifications.
